pedagogy.summary: Partitioning continuous shapes (circles, rectangles) into two and four EQUAL parts, naming them halves and quarters, and describing the whole as 'two halves' or 'four quarters'. The emphasis is on equal parts and on the part-whole relationship: the equal parts together reconstitute the whole. Children meet that a shape can be partitioned validly in more than one way, provided the parts are equal.
bestPractices: Partition by folding and cutting so equality is physical; verify by overlaying parts
Show more than one correct way to halve/quarter the same shape (e.g. a rectangle split vertically or horizontally) so 'halves' is not tied to one cut
Always recompose: 'two halves make the whole', 'four quarters make the whole'
Count the resulting PARTS (regions), not the cuts
Name as you go and have children label their partitions
keyRepresentations: Circles partitioned into 2 and 4 equal sectors
Rectangles partitioned into 2 and 4 equal parts (different orientations)
Overlay/rotation to check parts are equal
Parts reassembling into the whole shape
commonMisconceptions: Accepting unequal parts as halves/quarters because the number of pieces is right
Thinking a shape can only be partitioned one 'correct' way (rejecting valid alternative cuts)
Confusing the number of CUTS with the number of PARTS
Not seeing the whole as composed of its equal parts (cannot say two halves/four quarters make the whole)

learn.summary: Children partition continuous shapes (circles, rectangles) into two and four EQUAL parts, name them halves and quarters, and describe the whole as 'two halves' or 'four quarters'. The core ideas are equality of parts (equal in size, not necessarily the same shape), the part-whole relationship (equal parts recompose the whole), and that a shape can be partitioned validly in more than one way as long as the parts are equal.

activities.title: Cut it, check it, rebuild it
feedback: If parts don't match when overlaid, even after rotating or flipping them, they are not the same shape and size. For the strip, grid and straight-cut halves in this activity, that means they are not equal, so they are not halves/quarters even if the number of pieces looks right. (Pieces with equal area but different shapes, like the diagonal triangles below, need a different check.)
When a horizontal, vertical, or single-diagonal cut each produce two equal parts, each is a valid way to make halves: there is no single 'right' cut, only the equal-parts rule.

A rectangle can be quartered in more than one way too (four equal strips, or a 2x2 grid). Drawing BOTH diagonals also gives four triangles that each have one quarter of the AREA, but in a non-square rectangle they are different shapes and will not match when overlaid, so use strips or a 2x2 grid when you want quarters you can check by overlaying. Remember that equal parts must be the same SIZE, not necessarily the same shape.
After rebuilding, prompt: 'Two halves make what? Four quarters make what?' to rehearse the whole as composed of its equal parts.
Count the regions you ended up with, not the lines you drew: one cut through a shape makes two parts.
Real paper has slight thickness and cuts are never perfectly clean, so overlaying is a practical equality check; the cutouts stand for idealised flat shapes with zero thickness.
activities.rationale: Partitioning is a physical cutting/folding action; folding and overlaying makes equality concrete, showing several valid cuts confronts the 'only one correct way' misconception, and recomposing rehearses the part-whole relationship. Early fraction work centres on partitioning single objects into equal parts, naming them, and reconstituting the whole.
sourceClaims: Early fraction work partitions single objects into equal parts and names them (halves, quarters); equal parts and reconstituting the whole are central
Year 2 pupils recognise, name, and write fractions and can partition shapes; equal shares of identical wholes are emphasised
learnerActions: Take a paper circle and a paper rectangle and fold or draw a line to make two parts.
Overlay or rotate the two parts on top of each other to check they match exactly (equal).

On fresh copies of the same rectangle, make two halves a DIFFERENT way (e.g. vertically, then horizontally, then a single diagonal through opposite corners) and check equality again. For the diagonal, cut along it and turn one triangle half a turn to lay it on the other, because folding a non-square rectangle along its diagonal will not make the halves line up.
Now partition a circle and a rectangle into four equal parts (e.g. the rectangle as four equal strips or a 2x2 grid) and check all four match.
Slide or stick the parts back together to rebuild the whole, saying aloud 'two halves make the whole' and 'four quarters make the whole'.
Label each partition with 'halves' or 'quarters' and count the PARTS (regions), not the cuts.
activities.intendedInsight: Halves are two equal parts and quarters are four equal parts; the equal parts together rebuild the whole, and the same shape can be halved or quartered in more than one correct way provided the parts are equal in size.

activities.title: Halves, quarters, or neither?
feedback: A shape with two parts is only 'halves' if the two parts are equal: two unequal parts belong in 'neither'.
A rectangle cut by a single diagonal, or a circle halved by a slanted line through its centre, is still valid halves because the parts are equal.
Watch for judging by appearance of a usual cut: check equality directly by comparing part sizes.
A sorting task can check and teach how you classify partitions, but it does not itself give the experience of producing a partition; pair it with the cutting/folding activity.
activities.rationale: Categorising and matching partitions to names lets children apply the equal-parts rule and surfaces both the 'count the pieces' and 'only one correct cut' misconceptions through deliberate distractors. This is recognition practice that complements, rather than replaces, hands-on partitioning.
sourceClaims: Early fraction work partitions single objects into equal parts and names them (halves, quarters); equal parts and reconstituting the whole are central
learnerActions: Sort a set of partitioned shapes into three groups: 'halves', 'quarters', and 'neither'.
Include a shape split into two UNEQUAL parts (right number of pieces, wrong equality) to place in 'neither'.
Include a non-standard but valid cut (e.g. a diagonally-halved rectangle or a circle halved by a slanted line through its centre) to place in 'halves'.
For each decision, explain how you know, e.g. 'the parts are equal' or 'the parts are not the same size'.
activities.intendedInsight: Deciding whether a partition shows halves or quarters depends on whether the parts are equal in size, not on the number of pieces or on a familiar orientation.

activities.title: Diagnostic: unequal pieces with the right count
feedback: Neither shape is correctly cut: in each, the parts are not equal. Halves are two equal parts (for example, a straight line through the centre of a circle or rectangle); quarters are four equal parts.
Put back together, the four parts still make the whole rectangle, but because they are not equal they are not quarters; four equal quarters would also rebuild the whole rectangle.
A circle can be halved by any line through its centre, so there is more than one correct way.
If a child says 'yes, there are two parts so they are halves', overlay or rotate the parts to test equality and contrast an equal with an unequal partition of identical shapes.
activities.rationale: Both shapes have the right number of pieces but unequal sizes, so a piece-counting child says yes while a child requiring equal parts says no; the follow-up probes whether they see the parts recompose the whole and accept more than one valid partition.
sourceClaims: Early fraction work partitions single objects into equal parts and names them (halves, quarters); equal parts and reconstituting the whole are central
learnerActions: Look at a circle divided by an off-centre line into two clearly unequal parts, and a rectangle divided into four parts where three are small and one is large.
Answer: 'Is the circle cut into two halves? Is the rectangle cut into four quarters? How do you know?'
Then answer: 'If you put the parts of the rectangle back together, what do they make? Is there more than one way to cut the circle into two halves?'
activities.intendedInsight: Having the right NUMBER of pieces is not enough; halves and quarters must be EQUAL parts, which together recompose the whole, and there can be more than one valid partition.

constraints: Emphasise EQUAL parts throughout; a partition with the correct number of pieces but unequal sizes is not halves/quarters. Equal means equal in size, not necessarily the same shape.

Show more than one correct way to halve the same shape (e.g. a rectangle split vertically, horizontally, or by a single diagonal through opposite corners) and more than one way to quarter it (e.g. four equal strips or a 2x2 grid). Both diagonals of a rectangle also make four triangles of equal AREA (each one quarter), but for a non-square rectangle these triangles are not congruent, so they cannot be confirmed by overlaying - prefer strips or a 2x2 grid when children verify quarters by overlay.
Always recompose the whole: 'two halves make the whole', 'four quarters make the whole'.
Count the resulting PARTS (regions), not the cuts.
A sorting/matching task checks and can teach recognition and classification; it does not by itself give children the experience of producing partitions, so pair it with hands-on cutting/folding.
A poster or display of partitioned shapes is a useful reference but does not let a child partition and test equality themselves; treat it as a scaffold, not the main activity.
Paper cutouts have slight thickness and imperfect cuts; use overlaying as a practical equality check and treat the paper as an approximation of the idealised flat (zero-thickness) shape.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source noted '3D adds nothing' for these planar shapes; dropped as a universal claim. These shapes are plane figures so a solid model is not needed here, but that is a scope point, not evidence that 3D can never help.

An interactive version could shade equal parts green and unequal parts red, accept several valid halving cuts, and provide a 'rebuild' button that slides parts back and labels 'two halves'/'four quarters'. These are optional feedback mechanisms that make the equality check and recomposition concrete; they are not required.

The source labelled a conversation format 'poor' because this is a hands-on skill; spoken discussion while cutting (naming parts, explaining equality) remains valuable and is retained within the activities, so the format is not treated as useless.
Description mixes 'quarters' and 'fourths'; both name four equal parts and are used interchangeably here.

Corrected an earlier geometry error: both diagonals of a rectangle produce four triangles of EQUAL AREA (each a quarter), not unequal parts; for a non-square rectangle they are not congruent and so cannot be verified by overlay. A single diagonal is presented as a halving method because its two triangles are congruent and overlay-checkable. This reinforces that equal fractional parts must be equal in size, not identical in shape.

probeDeeper: Put the four pieces back together - what do you get?
Is there more than one way to cut this square into two halves? Show me another.
How is this different from just cutting it into any two pieces?
If I cut the rectangle into four equal parts, what is each part called, and what do all four make?
assess.correctAnswer: No to both - the parts are not equal. Halves are two equal parts (a line through the middle); quarters are four equal parts. Put back together, the four equal quarters make the whole rectangle, and a circle can be halved by any line through its centre (more than one way).

errorPatterns.pattern: The right number of pieces means the fraction - accepts unequal parts as halves/quarters
errorPatterns.nextMove: Overlay/rotate the parts to test equality; contrast an equal and an unequal partition of identical shapes.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes - there are two parts, so they are halves
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the unequal circle shows halves, or the unequal rectangle shows quarters

errorPatterns.pattern: Cannot describe the whole as composed of its equal parts (two halves / four quarters make the whole)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Physically reassemble the parts into the whole; rehearse 'four quarters make one whole'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Cannot answer what the parts make when reassembled

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks a shape can be partitioned only one 'correct' way (rejects a valid alternative cut)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show several equal partitions of the same shape side by side; the rule is equal parts, not a fixed cut.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says a horizontally- or diagonally-halved rectangle is 'wrong' because it isn't the usual vertical cut

responseLevels.gap: Accepts unequal parts as halves/quarters; counts pieces only.
responseLevels.full: Partitions circles and rectangles into equal halves and quarters, recognises different equal partitions are all valid, and describes the whole as composed of its equal parts.
responseLevels.partial: Identifies equal halves/quarters in the standard orientation but rejects valid alternative cuts, or cannot describe the whole as two halves / four quarters.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show a circle divided by an off-centre line into two clearly unequal parts, and a rectangle divided into four parts where three are small and one is large. Ask: 'Is the circle cut into two halves? Is the rectangle cut into four quarters? How do you know?' Then ask: 'If you put the parts of the rectangle back together, what do they make - and is there more than one way to cut the circle into two halves?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Both shapes have the RIGHT NUMBER of pieces but UNEQUAL sizes, so a child who counts pieces says yes while a child who requires equal parts says no. Tier 2 exposes whether they see the parts recompose the whole and accept more than one valid partition.
